questions.q: Identify the three primary physical locations in the story where the central conflict unfolds, and state one sensory detail associated with each.
questions.a: The three primary locations are: (1) Ramanand's moneylender/grocer shop — sensory detail: "oily hand" brushing the moustache, smell of grain/lentils implied by "lentil-eating shopkeeper"; (2) Khan Azam Khan's dilapidated Mughal-style house — sensory detail: "stately ruins," "faded remnants of a gold-brocaded waistcoat"; (3) The village tree where elders sit — sensory detail: landlord "preparing for a siesta," petition writer "smoking his hubble-bubble." A wrong answer listing only "village" or missing sensory details shows the student sees setting as a generic label, not a constructed space with texture.

questions.q: Explain how the social setting — the unwritten code linking moustache styles to class — functions as an invisible "law" that governs character behavior in the story.
questions.a: The moustache code acts as an invisible law because: (1) It dictates identity — Ramanand's goat moustache marks him as nouveau riche/commercial bourgeoisie; Khan's tiger moustache marks him as feudal gentry. (2) It triggers violence — the narrator mentions "rising ratio of murders" linked to "poaching on the style of one class by members of another." (3) It structures the conflict — Khan demands Ramanand lower his tips because the upturned tips "ape" the tiger style, violating class boundaries. (4) It enables economic exploitation — Ramanand uses the code to extract Khan's heirlooms by refusing to fully comply. A wrong answer treating moustaches as mere fashion misses that they are the physical manifestation of the social setting's rigid stratification.

questions.q: Apply the concept of "atmosphere shift" to the scene at Ramanand's shop: describe the atmosphere when Khan first enters, how it changes during the negotiation, and what specific textual evidence marks each shift.
questions.a: Atmosphere shifts in three stages: (1) Entry — tense, hostile: Khan asks "sourly," "Since when have the lentil-eating shopkeepers become noblemen?"; insults Ramanand as "seed of a donkey." (2) First negotiation — deceptively calm, transactional: Ramanand is "amenable," brushes one tip down "like a dead fly," says "Come, show me the trinkets." Khan becomes "soft wax," "humbly accepted the value." (3) Second confrontation — explosive, absurd: Khan notices the other tip still up, "raged," "roared," threatens to "wring your neck." Evidence: verbs shift from "asked sourly" to "humbly accepted" to "roared/spluttered." A wrong answer describing only "anger" misses the calculated manipulation by Ramanand that drives the shifts.

questions.q: Analyze how the description of Khan Azam Khan's house ("old dilapidated Moghul style house," "stately ruins") creates an atmosphere of ironic pathos that deepens the story's satire on class pride.
questions.a: The house description creates ironic pathos through contrast: (1) "Moghul style" and "ancient Afghan family" evoke grandeur; "dilapidated," "hasn't even a patch of land left," "tottering house" reveal destitution. (2) "Stately ruins around Khan Azam Khan what grace was once his" — the setting visually embodies the gap between inherited pride and present reality. (3) This irony fuels the satire: Khan guards "every sacred brick" against vandalism while pawning his wife's nose-ring, then heirlooms. The house is a physical metaphor for the tiger moustache — a magnificent symbol with no material foundation. A wrong answer calling it "sad" or "poor" misses the irony: the setting mocks the very pride it houses.

questions.q: Evaluate whether the final atmosphere of the story — the peasants laughing, Khan twisting his moustache "maintaining the valiant uprightness" — is ultimately comic, tragic, or both. Justify with two pieces of evidence.
questions.a: The final atmosphere is both comic and tragic (tragicomedy). Comic: peasants "laughed to see the Khan," Ramanand mutters "My father was a Sultan" mocking Khan's lineage, the absurdity of a deed signed over a moustache tip. Tragic: Khan loses "all his remaining worldly possessions, my pots and pans, my clothes, even my house" for a symbolic gesture; he walks away a "pauper" clinging to "the symbol of his ancient and noble family." The tragedy is that the class system forces him to choose between survival and dignity; the comedy is that the system is so fragile a moneylender can manipulate it with a greasy hand. A wrong answer picking only one tone fails to see Anand's dual vision: he laughs at the absurdity while mourning the human cost.

questions.q: Create a 50-word micro-fiction scene set in the same village, ten years later, where the moustache code has changed or collapsed. Use at least one sensory detail from the original story.
questions.a: A strong answer will: (1) Place the scene in a recognizable location (shop, tree, Khan's house ruins), (2) Show a changed social code (e.g., clean-shaven youth, moustaches as fashion not law), (3) Include a sensory echo (oil, hubble-bubble, lentils, gold brocade), (4) Imply the economic shift (landlord gone, moneylender's shop modernized). Example: "The shop smelled of packaged oil, not grain. Ramanand's grandson, clean-shaven, scanned UPI codes. Under the tree, no elders smoked hubble-bubbles — only teens scrolling phones. Khan's house was a tea-stall; his tiger moustache, a faded photo on the wall. The deed? Framed as a joke." A weak answer ignores the original's sensory world or treats the code as still absolute, missing the story's implied impermanence.
